item.title: ... Remembering Rodney Dangerfield...
item.description: On October 5, 2004, Rodney Dangerfield died at UCLA Medical Center at 82 after complications from heart surgery. The comedian who joked that nobody respected him left behind a wife, two children, and a career built almost entirely on rejection. Born Jacob Rodney Cohen on November 22, 1921, in Deer Park, New York, Rodney grew up with instability close by. His father, Philip Cohen, performed in vaudeville and was often absent. After his parents separated, Rodney lived mainly with his mother and sister. Money was tight, affection could be scarce, and humor became one of the ways he learned to survive uncomfortable rooms. By his teens, he was already writing jokes. At 19, he began performing under the name Jack Roy, working small clubs and struggling for attention. The laughs were inconsistent and the money was worse. He married Joyce Indig in 1949, and the need to support a family eventually pushed comedy aside. For years, the future star sold aluminum siding and worked ordinary jobs while raising his children, Melanie and Brian. He later joked about how badly business treated him, but the deeper truth was less funny. He had tried show business, failed to break through, and walked away while still young enough to wonder whether the dream had been foolish. Then, in his forties, he returned. The second attempt was different. He had a new name, Rodney Dangerfield, and a comic identity built around humiliation. The suit was slightly wrong, the collar always seemed too tight, his eyes looked permanently worried, and every sentence sounded like another insult had just landed. The phrase “I don’t get no respect” became his engine. His breakthrough came on "The Ed Sullivan Show" in 1967. Dangerfield was already 45, an age when many entertainers are protecting established careers, not beginning one. Television audiences immediately understood the character. He was the man whose doctor, wife, neighbors, and even pets seemed to dislike him. "The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson" gave him an even larger stage. Dangerfield appeared dozens of times, firing off jokes at a speed that made embarrassment feel triumphant. The rejection that had once driven him out of comedy had become the material people now waited to hear. In 1969, he opened Dangerfield’s comedy club in Manhattan. It became more than a business. The room gave younger comics a place to work, fail, adjust, and come back. Dangerfield knew exactly what it felt like to need another chance because his own career had depended on one. Movies widened his audience again. In "Caddyshack" (1980), he played Al Czervik, the loud, wealthy outsider who shattered the country club’s stiffness. In "Easy Money" (1983), he played a man forced to change his habits for an inheritance. Then "Back to School" (1986) made him a leading man in his sixties as Thornton Melon, a rich father who enrolls in college beside his son. The success came late enough that Rodney could never completely forget the years nobody cared. He won a Grammy for his comedy album "No Respect," hosted television specials, and became one of the most recognizable stand-up comedians in America. Yet the act still depended on the old wound. The louder the crowd laughed, the more Rodney insisted the world had overlooked him. His private life had its own turns. Rodney and Joyce divorced, remarried, then separated permanently. In 1993, he married Joan Child, who stayed with him through his final years and serious health problems. By 2004, heart trouble had become severe. Before surgery, Dangerfield was still joking. Asked how long he might be hospitalized, he answered, “If all goes well, about a week. If not, about an hour and a half.” He underwent heart valve replacement surgery, fell into a coma afterward, and never fully recovered.

item.title: Apparently Fucking Taxes Are Only Mandatory If You’re Too Poor to Call Them an “Experiment”
item.description:
Apparently we've discovered a fascinating new feature of the tax code: If you're an ordinary person, it's a tax bill. If you're a gigantic tech company building a massive data center, apparently you just need enough lawyers to ask: “But what if we call it an experiment?” Fucking brilliant.
You couldn't pull this shit. Try telling the government your house isn't actually a house. It's a long-term experimental residential computing environment containing a refrigerator and two bedrooms. Therefore property taxes shouldn't apply. Please let me know how the audit goes. But scale the project up until it consumes staggering amounts of electricity, water, land and infrastructure… …and suddenly we're discussing exemptions, incentives, classifications and tax structures worth potentially tens of billions of dollars. Funny how complicated taxation becomes once you're rich enough. And that's what makes the reported $75 BILLION figure so fucking staggering. Not because somebody necessarily stuffed $75 billion into a suitcase marked TAXES WE STOLE. It's about the enormous value potentially at stake when these facilities qualify for favorable tax treatment. Still feeling experimental? Meanwhile: You miss $600 of income? Explain yourself. You make a mistake on your taxes? Fix it. You owe money? Pay up. Multibillion-dollar corporation builds an industrial complex the size of fucking Mordor? “Well, technically, we'd prefer to discuss the definition of ‘data center.’” And let's remember what these facilities actually require. Electricity. Water. Roads. Transmission infrastructure. Communities capable of supporting them. All the boring public shit society somehow manages to understand perfectly well when it's time for taxpayers to fund it. I'm all for experimentation. So here's one: Build enormously profitable infrastructure. Use public resources. Make billions. Then pay the same fucking taxes everyone else is expected to pay. Crazy concept, I know. We could call it: THE ACCOUNTABILITY EXPERIMENT. #BigTech #DataCenters #Taxes #TaxBreaks #CorporateWelfare #AI #Tech #Amazon #Meta #Microsoft #Google #WorkingClass #Taxpayers #PoliticalSatire #CorporateAmerica #Accountability

item.title: Real Confession
item.description: I gave up the past 15 years of my life to taking care of my grandmother. I never regretted a minute of it and until the start of this year I was able to do it with a smile and being comforting to her. This year has been the hardest year of my life and it just got harder. Gram has started lashing out, having more and more hallucinations, and can barely walk. She tried taking pills whenever she wanted which caused me to have to move her pills so she doesn't OD. I talked it through with her so she knows where they are and why. Tonight she suddenly got mad that I had her pills and said she would purposefully not take the pills I give her. Then she said she hopes she gets sick so she can blame it on me to her doctor. I know this isn't the grandmother I knew, I know it is the late stage dementia....but knowing something doesn't stop the pain. Now I am going to have to quit my job because I can't work and full time care give...I can't even sleep as she will try to sneak around when I go to bed. I tried writing, drawing, and game development but I don't get to have a life while I am maintaining hers. I have $0 in the bank and nothing to show for my life. "I'm just afraid that if I died today, my life would have amounted to nothing." Sorry to be a Debbie downer, it is just making my physically ill (constantly nauseating).
